e: From ischium + crus + -al, an occasional coinage gradually gaining ground over the 20th century.
From New Latin ischaemiae, from ischaemia + Latin -ae (the nominative plural form of -a (suffix forming agent nouns)).
Latin ischuria, Ancient Greek ἰσχουρία (iskhouría, “retention of urine”), from ἴσχω (ískhō, “to keep back, restrain”) + οὖρον (oûron, “urine”).
17th century, from Latin ischium, from Ancient Greek ἰσχίον (iskhíon, “hip joint”).
q: And he still carried, after five or six years, and though he dressed it in a mirror night and morning, on his right ischium a running sore of traumatic origin.

e: From Ancient Greek ἴσχιον (ískhion, “hip”) + πάγος (págos, “fixed, set”) (from πήγνυμι (pḗgnumi, “fasten, fix, set”)); equivalent to ischio- + -pagus.
From New Latin ischialgia, from Latin ischion + -algia.
Combining form of Ancient Greek ἰσχίον (iskhíon, “ischium”).
From Ancient Greek ἴσχειν (ískhein, “hold back”) + hidrosis (“excessive sweat”).

From New Latin ischaemia, from Ancient Greek ἴσχαιμος (ískhaimos, “stoppage of blood flow”), from ῐ̓́σχω (ĭ́skhō, “to hold back, restrain; to stay, stop”) + αἷμᾰ (haîmă, “blood”).
The plural form ischemiae is also from New Latin ischaemiae.

q: The remedy was tried in rheumatic joint affections, neuralgias of the same nature, and especially ischiagra.
